title: A Soviet Animation of Stephen King’s Short Story “Battleground” (1986)
description:
in Animation, Literature |   	October 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Stephen King has that rare, and spec­tac­u­lar­ly prof­itable, skill to
body:
in Animation, Literature |   	October 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Stephen King has that rare, and spec­tac­u­lar­ly prof­itable, skill to suck you into his world and com­pel you to flip to the next page. And when you’re hooked, his words have the uncan­ny abil­i­ty to sim­ply unfold like a movie in your head. So it isn’t sur­pris­ing that his books have been wide­ly adapt­ed to the sil­ver screen. Some are flat out mas­ter­pieces. Oth­ers are most decid­ed­ly not. This appre­ci­a­tion by film­mak­ers of King’s sto­ry­telling chops isn’t just con­tained to this side of the Iron Cur­tain. In 1986, Sovi­et ani­ma­tor Mikhail Titov — whose pre­vi­ous work includes How the Cos­sacks Played Foot­ball (1970) — turned King’s short sto­ry “Bat­tle­ground” (1972) into an ani­mat­ed movie, titled sim­ply Сражение or Bat­tle.
The short is about a noirish hired gun who dress­es in a trench coat and a fedo­ra. He is con­tract­ed to kill a toy mak­er. When he returns home, he dis­cov­ers that there’s a box on his doorstep and makes the com­plete­ly unwise deci­sion of tak­ing it inside. Soon, toy sol­diers start to tum­ble out of the box. They have live ammo, rock­et launch­ers, tiny lit­tle heli­copters at their dis­pos­al and they are on a sin­gle-mind­ed mis­sion to kill him. The killer soon finds him­self pinned down in the bath­room, wait­ing for the next attack.
The film is a lot of fun. Titov relies heav­i­ly on roto­scop­ing – an ani­ma­tion tech­nique you prob­a­bly remem­ber from A‑ha’s music video Take On Me. The killer’s form and move­ments feel real­is­tic as the rest of the movie’s height­ened, brood­ing world bends and bulges as if ren­dered through a fish­eye lens. And like A‑ha, the film’s synth and sax­o­phone sound­track might sound painful­ly 80s to some. You can watch Bat­tle with sub­ti­tles above or with­out sub­ti­tles below. The dia­logue is min­i­mal through­out.


	

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2014.

title: How Balzac’s Extreme Coffee Habit Fueled His Productive Writing Routine
description:
in History, Literature |   	October 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Even now, in this age when the very read­ing of lit­er­a­ture is endan­gered —
body:
in History, Literature |   	October 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Even now, in this age when the very read­ing of lit­er­a­ture is endan­gered — or so the arti­cles tell us — Hon­oré de Balzac (1799–1850) retains a notable abil­i­ty to pick up new admir­ers. But even though he may have a decent read­er­ship by the stan­dards of French nov­el­ists who died in the mid­dle of the nine­teenth cen­tu­ry, one does won­der whether he still inspires the kind of devo­tion embod­ied by William Hobart Royce. A Brook­lyn book­seller’s assis­tant first intro­duced to Les Cent Con­tes dro­la­tiques as an impres­sion­able (and duly scan­dal­ized) teenag­er on a trip to Eng­land, Royce became not just the ear­ly twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry’s fore­most Amer­i­can expert on Balzac, but also a kind of clone of the man him­self, right down to his appear­ance.
“In their long asso­ci­a­tion, Royce has con­tract­ed sev­er­al habits from Balzac,” writes the New York­er’s Alva John­ston in a 1933 pro­file. “When work­ing late at night or ear­ly in the morn­ing, he com­bats fatigue, as Balzac did, by tak­ing snuff, smok­ing Latakia tobac­co, and drink­ing enor­mous quan­ti­ties of cof­fee. These are not mere whims or idol-wor­ship­ping cer­e­monies on the part of Royce; they are prac­tices which he adopt­ed from Balzac after test­ing them and con­vinc­ing him­self that they were sound.”
Balzac him­self explains the impor­tance of these sub­stances to the writ­ing life — noth­ing less, to his mind, than life itself — in “Traité des exci­tants mod­ernes,” or “Trea­tise on Mod­ern Stim­u­lants,” an essay he append­ed to Phys­i­olo­gie du goût, the cel­e­brat­ed text by the lawyer-politi­cian-gour­mand Jean Anthelme Bril­lat-Savarin.

Known for drink­ing his own cus­tom blend of beans from Mar­tinique, cof­fee from Bour­bon (now known as Réu­nion Island), and Mokha from the pot pic­tured above, Balzac also rec­om­mends to his fel­low “men of exces­sive vig­or” a “hor­ri­ble, rather bru­tal method” involv­ing “fine­ly pul­ver­ized, dense cof­fee” pre­pared with as lit­tle water as pos­si­ble and con­sumed on an emp­ty stom­ach. In response, he promis­es in this par­tial Eng­lish trans­la­tion of the essay, “ideas quick march into motion like bat­tal­ions of a grand army to its leg­endary fight­ing ground, and the bat­tle rages. Mem­o­ries charge in, bright flags on high; the cav­al­ry of metaphor deploys with a mag­nif­i­cent gal­lop; the artillery of log­ic rush­es up with clat­ter­ing wag­ons and car­tridges; on imagination’s orders, sharp­shoot­ers sight and fire; forms and shapes and char­ac­ters rear up.”
In the case of Balzac, who cre­at­ed thou­sands of char­ac­ters and deployed them across his body of work, that charge could have been a fear­some sight indeed. Yet he proved equal to it night after writ­ing night, sit­ting down to his desk some time between mid­night and 2:00 a.m., then pro­duc­ing man­u­script pages with his quill at a type­writer’s pace until morn­ing. After a nap, more work fol­lowed until 4:00 or so in the after­noon; soon there­after would come an ear­ly-evening din­ner, and thus the cycle would repeat. A com­mon­ly cit­ed fig­ure holds that Balzac drank as many as 50 cups of cof­fee per day, which even the most proud­ly caf­feine-hooked lap­top jock­ey today would strug­gle to touch. Nor would it be advis­able to try, giv­en that Balza­c’s for­mi­da­ble cof­fee habit may have con­tributed to his death at age 51 — but then, it cer­tain­ly played a part in the pro­duc­tiv­i­ty that ensured his immor­tal­ité.

title: Inside the Making of the Sagrada Família, Barcelona’s 144-Year Megaproject
description: To get a sense of Sagra­da Famíli­a’s pop­u­lar­i­ty with YouTu­bers, you have only to take a look at the relat­ed Open Cul­ture posts linked
body:
To get a sense of Sagra­da Famíli­a’s pop­u­lar­i­ty with YouTu­bers, you have only to take a look at the relat­ed Open Cul­ture posts linked below. As will hard­ly escape your atten­tion, most sub­jects that con­sis­tent­ly draw the atten­tion of the GoPro class are not nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry Catholic church­es. But Antoni Gaudí’s mas­ter­piece, whose con­struc­tion alone has sur­vived him by a cen­tu­ry now, tran­scends many bound­aries of intel­lec­tu­al and cul­tur­al inter­est: his­to­ry chan­nels fea­ture it, trav­el chan­nels fea­ture it, reli­gious chan­nels fea­ture it, and, of course, archi­tec­ture chan­nels fea­ture it. Most recent­ly, Sagra­da Família has appeared on The B1M, which is all about con­struc­tion — the more ambi­tious, the bet­ter.
We’ve pre­vi­ous­ly post­ed B1M videos on the Flat­iron Build­ing, the Guggen­heim Muse­um Bil­bao, the extrater­res­tri­al­ly curv­ing work of Zaha Hadid, and every gen­er­a­tion of New York sky­scraper. That selec­tion only hints at the range of struc­tures to which the chan­nel’s cre­ator Fred Mills has paid close atten­tion, and yet it’s Sagra­da Família that puts him at a loss. “There’s parts of this build­ing where you can’t help but describe what you’re see­ing,” he says as he stands in its stained glass-illu­mi­nat­ed cen­tral nave. “There’s oth­er moments where you don’t have the words; it’s just emo­tion.” Enter­ing it feels, as he describes it, “less like you’re stand­ing inside a build­ing, and more like you’ve been trans­port­ed to the thresh­old of heav­en itself.”
How does Sagra­da Família cre­ate this expe­ri­ence for its vis­i­tors, even in its incom­plete state? Some will cred­it divine inspi­ra­tion; oth­ers, Gaudí’s sheer archi­tec­tur­al genius. Mills seeks out more con­crete forms of expla­na­tion, right down to the very blocks of stone used to build its tow­ers. Grant­ed much more access than ordi­nary tourists, who now come at a rate of about 1,500 per hour, he goes all the way up to see the mas­sive cross assem­bled on the church’s pin­na­cle, and all the way down to the base­ment work­shop where intri­cate mod­els test the myr­i­ad pos­si­ble ways to real­ize Gaudí’s vision. For when he died in 1926, hav­ing been hit by a tram, the plans he left behind did­n’t exact­ly explain all the details about how to fin­ish what resem­bled no oth­er build­ing ever erect­ed, reli­gious or oth­er­wise.
As Mills points out, sub­se­quent­ly devel­oped tech­nolo­gies have helped keep Sagra­da Famíli­a’s now 144-year-long con­struc­tion pro­ceed­ing apace. And though great cel­e­bra­tion attend­ed the top­ping-out of its cen­tral tow­er high above the streets of Barcelona this past Feb­ru­ary, more work remains to be done. Com­plet­ing its inte­ri­or, roofs, and side chapels, as well as the grand façade with its main entrance, should take anoth­er decade, depend­ing on how the rel­e­vant dis­putes involv­ing local res­i­dents and the city coun­cil play out. Still, it seems like­ly indeed that Sagra­da Família will final­ly be fin­ished with­in our life­times, which makes for the kind of dra­ma that will keep attract­ing both large- and small-time doc­u­men­tar­i­ans. “I’m not sure we’re ever going to see any­thing else quite like it,” Mills says, which hints at anoth­er rea­son for all the con­tent-cre­ator fas­ci­na­tion: though it may well be com­plet­ed in our age, Sagra­da Família could hard­ly be less of our age.

title: The Vibrant Color Wheels Designed by Goethe, Newton & Other Theorists of Color (1665–1810)
description: Maybe it’s the clois­tered headi­ness of Rene Descartes, or the rig­or­ous aus­ter­i­ty of Isaac New­ton; maybe it’s all the leath­ern breech­es,
body:
Maybe it’s the clois­tered headi­ness of Rene Descartes, or the rig­or­ous aus­ter­i­ty of Isaac New­ton; maybe it’s all the leath­ern breech­es, gray waist­coats, sal­low faces, and pow­dered wigs… but we tend not to asso­ciate Enlight­en­ment Europe with an explo­sion of col­or the­o­ry. Yet philoso­phers of the late 17th and 18th cen­turies were obsessed with light and sight. Descartes wrote a trea­tise on optics, as did New­ton.
New­ton first described in his 1672 paper the “rev­o­lu­tion­ary new the­o­ry of light and colour,” the Uni­ver­si­ty of Cam­bridge Whip­ple Library writes, “in which he claimed that exper­i­ments with prisms proved that white light was com­prised of light of sev­en dis­tinct colours.” Sci­en­tists debat­ed Newton’s the­o­ry “well into the 19th cen­tu­ry.”

One ear­ly oppo­nent famous­ly illus­trat­ed his rebut­tal. Poet, writer, and sci­en­tist Johann Wolf­gang von Goethe pub­lished The­o­ry of Col­ors (see here), with its care­ful­ly hand-drawn and col­ored dia­grams and wheels, in 1810. From New­ton’s time onward, col­or the­o­rists elab­o­rat­ed pre­vail­ing con­cepts with col­or wheels, the first attrib­uted to New­ton in 1704 (and drawn in black and white, above).

Newton’s wheel “arranged red, orange, yel­low, green, blue, indi­go, and vio­let into a nat­ur­al pro­gres­sion on a rotat­ing disk.” A few years lat­er, two col­or circles—one with 7 col­ors and anoth­er with 12—appeared in a paint­ing man­u­al attrib­uted to Claude Boutet (top), based on Newton’s the­o­ries. Artists, chemists, map­mak­ers, poets, even ento­mol­o­gists… every­one seemed to have a pet the­o­ry of col­or, gen­er­al­ly accom­pa­nied by elab­o­rate col­ored charts and dia­grams.

The col­or wheel was one among many forms—which often pre­sent­ed con­trast­ing the­o­ries, like that of Jacques-Fabi­en Gau­ti­er, who argued that black and white were pri­ma­ry col­ors. But the wheel, and Newton’s basic ideas about it, have endured almost unchanged. The wheel fur­ther up (third one from top) by British ento­mol­o­gist Moses Har­ris from 1766 shows Newton’s 7‑color scheme sim­pli­fied to the 6 pri­ma­ry and sec­ondary col­ors we usu­al­ly see, arranged in the com­ple­men­tary and anal­o­gous scheme, with ter­tiary gra­da­tions between them. Anoth­er ento­mol­o­gist, Ignaz Schif­fer­müller, drew the 12-col­or wheel right above.

Col­or is always rep­re­sen­ta­tive. Newton’s orig­i­nal wheel includ­ed “musi­cal notes cor­re­lat­ed with col­or.” By the end of the 18th cen­tu­ry, col­or the­o­ry had become increas­ing­ly tied to psy­cho­log­i­cal the­o­ries and typolo­gies, as in the wheel above, the “rose of tem­pera­ments,” made by Goethe and Friedrich Schiller in 1799 to illus­trate “human occu­pa­tions and char­ac­ter traits,” the Pub­lic Domain Review notes, includ­ing “tyrants, heroes, adven­tur­ers, hedo­nists, lovers, poets, pub­lic speak­ers, his­to­ri­ans, teach­ers, philoso­phers, pedants, rulers,” grouped into the four tem­pera­ments of humoral the­o­ry.

It’s a fair­ly short leap from these psy­cholo­gies of col­or to those used by adver­tis­ers and com­mer­cial design­ers in the 20th century—or from the artists and sci­en­tists’ col­or the­o­ries to abstract expres­sion­ism, the Bauhaus school, and the chemists and pho­tog­ra­phers who recre­at­ed the col­ors of the world on film. (Goethe’s col­or wheel, below, from The­o­ry of Col­ors, illus­trates his chap­ter on “Alle­gor­i­cal, sym­bol­ic, and mys­ti­cal use of colour.”) See more ear­ly col­or wheels, like Philipp Otto Runge’s 1810 Far­benkugel, as well as oth­er con­cep­tu­al col­or schemes, at the Pub­lic Domain Review.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

description:
All images courtesy of Zebu, shared with permission
October 27, 2026


For more than a decade, Berlin-based artists Lynn Lehmann and Dennis Gärtner,
body:
All images courtesy of Zebu, shared with permission
October 27, 2026


For more than a decade, Berlin-based artists Lynn Lehmann and Dennis Gärtner, a.k.a. Zebu, have been transforming otherwise mundane walls and surfaces into vivid, geometric paintings. Moving between patterns and representational abstraction, the duo draw on their adjacent work in illustration and graphic design to create eye-popping compositions. Indeed, much of their practice is studio-based, so murals introduce broader possibilities in a variety of settings. “There’s something special about being able to interrupt someone’s everyday routine with an unexpected visual surprise,” the pair says.
Currently, Zebu is experimenting with a more intuitive approach to murals as a complement to their method if planning extensively beforehand. “It’s been a really exciting and surprising experience that has taught us to trust the process more and brought back a lot of the fun of painting.” See more on Zebu’s Instagram.

title: A Macro Journey Underwater Reveals the Radiant Geometries of Coral
description: Armed with high-magnification macro lenses, filmmaker Sandro Bocci journeyed through coral reefs to document a striking array of color, texture, a
body:
Armed with high-magnification macro lenses, filmmaker Sandro Bocci journeyed through coral reefs to document a striking array of color, texture, and pattern. A project for Bocci’s collective Julia Set Lab, the short film homes in on the intricacies of a life form we can’t see with the naked eye. Subtle shifts in gradients, bold color juxtapositions, and a seemingly endless diversity of recurring motifs explode across the frame, revealing the beauty and complexity of the extraordinary organisms growing below the water’s surface.
Set to music by Maurizio Morganti, “Iteration” is the second collaboration by the pair, who continue to harness the power of technology to create works at the intersection of art and science. Watch the film on Vimeo, along with additional films.

title: Tom Hegen's 'The Mineral Age' Documents the Indelible Effects of the Green Transition
description: In its current form, the global transition away from fossil fuels will depend on the earth’s rare minerals. According to ClimateWorks, we’ll colle
body:
In its current form, the global transition away from fossil fuels will depend on the earth’s rare minerals. According to ClimateWorks, we’ll collectively need to mine 6.5 billion tons of cobalt, copper, lithium, nickel, and other materials before 2050 in order to keep up with energy demands. Most of these resources are found in regions already facing the greatest impacts of the climate crisis, from Chile’s Atacama Desert to Indonesia’s nickel reserves to the cobalt deposits of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
For the past six years, German photographer Tom Hegen has been traveling the globe to document the communities bearing the brunt of this transition. Through his signature aerial images, Hegen captures the landscapes and communities transformed by such extractions, which he presents in his new book, The Mineral Age.
Evaporation ponds for lithium production, Atacama Desert, Antofagasta Region, Chile, 2021
“What particularly caught my attention was that many of these resources are concentrated in just a handful of countries, creating new geopolitical dependencies and vulnerabilities,” Hegen tells Colossal. “At the same time, their extraction often comes with significant environmental and social consequences that receive relatively little public attention.” 
The Mineral Age redresses that omission through 247 photographs revealing the indelible effects of mining. We bear witness to the candy-colored evaporation ponds needed to harvest lithium in the Atacama Desert, along with an ochre-tinged nickel pit jutting up against a rainforest in Sulawesi, Indonesia. “Moving away from fossil fuels is far more complex than we might initially imagine. I firmly believe that decarbonising our economies and societies is essential to addressing climate change,” he adds. “The pressing question, however, is at what cost—and who ultimately bears that cost?”
Hegen echoes the concerns of communities around the world, including those of the Salinas Grandes in the Atacama Desert. We recently wrote about the collaborative project helmed by Argentinian artist Tomás Saraceno, who’s been collaborating with Indigenous peoples in the region for decades as they protest lithium mining. Together, they’re working to preserve the ancestral homelands and the resources held underground. Revealing the impacts from the air, The Mineral Age is a converse to Saraceno’s project, which is embedded in the land itself.
“One of the most important lessons I’ve taken from this project is that no source of energy comes entirely without environmental or social consequences,” Hegen says. “Even technologies we consider clean or renewable depend on extensive industrial processes, vast amounts of raw materials, and the extraction of finite resources.”
Nickel open-pit mine encroaching on primary rainforest, Sulawesi, Indonesia, 2025
Like Saraceno, Hegen also emphasizes that this conversation isn’t about whether we need to abandon fossil fuels—both agree we do—but rather about how we can do so without replicating the same harmful, extractive policies of our current system.
Published by Hatje Cantz, The Mineral Age is available for pre-order on Bookshop or through Kickstarter. Follow his latest projects on Instagram.
